analysis.one_liner: Raises the bar for police to seize and keep property without a criminal conviction.
analysis.headline: Introduced on February 20, 2026 with sponsors from both parties, the bill has sat without action in four House committees and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Civil asset forfeiture lets federal agents take cash, cars, homes, and bank accounts when they suspect a crime, without ever charging or convicting the owner. This bill would make the government prove its case with clear and convincing evidence instead of the lower standard it uses now, notify owners within 7 days of a seizure instead of 60, appoint a lawyer for owners who cannot afford one, close the loophole that lets agencies keep property without going to court, and give owners of seized bank accounts a quick hearing. It would also stop agencies from sharing forfeiture proceeds with state and local police and send the money to the Treasury instead of back into law-enforcement budgets.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose property is seized, and anyone at risk of having cash, a car, a home, or a bank account taken on mere suspicion. Under current law, the government can win a forfeiture by a preponderance of the evidence, notice can lag 60 days, and owners who cannot afford a lawyer may fight the government alone or give up because the lawyer costs more than the property. The bill flips the burden and the odds in the owner's favor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose cash or property gets seized

how_it_helps.text: Raises the government's burden of proof in every civil forfeiture from a preponderance of the evidence to clear and convincing evidence, and requires proof of a substantial connection between the property and the offense [S2] [S3].

Shortens the deadline to notify owners of a seizure from 60 days to 7 days, and shortens the deadline for the government to file its case from 90 days after a claim is filed to 30 days after the seizure [S2] [S3].
Allows courts to appoint counsel for owners who are financially unable to hire a lawyer, or for whom a lawyer would cost more than the seized property is worth [S2] [S3].
Bars nonjudicial forfeitures entirely: no federal agency could take property except through a proceeding before a United States district court [S3].

Gives owners of money seized over alleged structuring (splitting deposits to dodge reporting rules) a court hearing within 14 days, with the property returned unless the government shows probable cause; structuring seizures are a common way small-business owners' bank accounts are drained [S2] [S3].

Directs forfeiture proceeds to the Treasury's general fund instead of the DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund, and eliminates the equitable-sharing program that sends federal forfeiture money to state and local police agencies, removing the financial incentive agencies have to seize property [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal law-enforcement agencies and their state and local partners, who would lose the seizure revenue they currently keep and use for their own budgets. Agencies would also face more work per case: judicial proceedings instead of administrative paperwork, faster deadlines, and a higher standard of proof. Taxpayers collectively would not pay; the money simply stops flowing to agencies and goes to the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: Prosecutors and law-enforcement groups argue that forfeiture, including equitable sharing, is a key tool against drug trafficking and organized crime, and that raising the standard of proof and eliminating nonjudicial forfeiture would let criminal networks shield proceeds from seizure [S2].
State and local police departments would lose funds they currently receive through equitable sharing, which some departments rely on to buy equipment and fund operations [S2].
Appointing counsel at government expense for every indigent owner who contests a forfeiture adds a cost the bill does not offset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: ordinary people get meaningful protection against losing property without a criminal conviction, while law-enforcement agencies lose a funding stream and an enforcement shortcut. The main good-faith objection is that some legitimate seizures of criminal proceeds become harder; the counterargument is that under current law innocent owners already bear that cost, since they must win a legal fight to get their own property back. The bill applies retroactively to pending cases, which compounds the burden on agencies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and immediately referred to four committees at once, and none of them has acted on it; no vote has been scheduled and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 20, 2026 by Rep. Tim Walberg with Reps. Jamie Raskin, Tom McClintock, and Mary Gay Scanlon as original cosponsors, making its original lineup bipartisan (two Democrats, two Republicans) [S3] [S4].
It was referred the same day to four committees at once: Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Financial Services [S1] [S5].
No committee has reported the bill, no vote has been held, and no further action has been taken since the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law-enforcement agencies keep the current rules, including seizure revenue that flows back into their own budgets, because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law-enforcement agencies, under the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill's original lineup was evenly bipartisan: a Republican sponsor joined by two Democrats and one Republican, and no party has acted against it on the record yet.

industries.industry: Federal law-enforcement agencies (DOJ and its components)
industries.note: Agencies currently deposit forfeiture proceeds into the DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund and can spend them directly. The bill reroutes that money to the Treasury's general fund, ending the arrangement under which seizures fund the agencies doing the seizing [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: State, local, and tribal police departments
industries.note: Equitable sharing currently passes federal forfeiture money to these agencies that assist in investigations. The bill eliminates that authority, removing a revenue stream departments have used to fund equipment and operations [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With four simultaneous committee referrals and zero action in the months since introduction, the bill faces long odds: civil forfeiture reform bills in this family have repeatedly died in committee in past Congresses despite bipartisan sponsorship. It would need a committee to move first and leadership to schedule floor time, neither of which has happened.
